source: Bradley (2019) Imprecise Probabilities, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
finding: Replace one probability function with a set P (a representor or credal set). Lower and upper envelopes are inf and sup of P(X). Updating is done member by member. The envelopes alone lose information.
numbers: Upper(X) = 1 - Lower(not X). Update rule: P(X|E) = {p(X|E): p in P, p(E)>0}.
limits: The article warns that the summary interval is not an adequate picture of the belief state. Walley 1991 and Levi 1980 are cited there; those primary books were not opened.
agent_relevance: A cheap data structure for an 'unknown' flag: store a low and a high value, not a point. The interval alone is not the full state.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, section 2.1 Ellsberg decisions
finding: The 90-ball urn: 30 red, 60 blue or yellow in unknown mix. Preferring bet I (red) to II (blue) and IV (not red) to III (not blue) cannot fit any single probability. Imprecise model: P(R)=1/3, P(B)=P(Y)=[0,2/3].
numbers: Bets: I=R, II=B, III=R or Y, IV=B or Y. Single probability needs r>b and r+y<y+b, which is impossible.
limits: SEP says some experiments find Ellsberg patterns rarer than assumed (Binmore et al. 2012; Voorhoeve et al. 2016). Steele (2007): the IP rationale works only for genuinely indeterminate beliefs, not for poorly introspected precise ones.
agent_relevance: An agent that gets a number from a model cannot tell 'known 1/3' from 'unknown in [0,2/3]'. Keep that difference when two options have the same point estimate.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, section 3.1 Dilation
finding: Dilation: after learning evidence, the interval can get wider than before, even for evidence that seems irrelevant. White's coin puzzle: P(H)={1/2} but P(H|Y)=[0,1].
numbers: Prior P(H)=1/2 exactly; posterior [0,1] after seeing which side of the painted coin is up.
limits: Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993 proved the general pattern (cited, not opened). Some authors accept dilation as correct, others use it to attack IP.
agent_relevance: A wide interval may legitimately grow after new input. Do not treat 'interval widened' as an error signal by default.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, section 3.2 Belief inertia
finding: With a vacuous prior P(H1)=[0,1], every posterior is also [0,1] for any evidence, so you never learn. Levi (1980, ch. 13) raised this. Walley accepted it: vacuous previsions are trivial models, and near-vacuous priors work.
numbers: Formula: p(H1|E) = p1 p(H1) / (p2 + (p1-p2) p(H1)); continuous in the prior, so the whole [0,1] range is reached.
limits: Fixes proposed: Rinard (2013) bans vacuous priors; Wilson 2001 and Cattaneo 2008, 2014 cut priors that gave tiny likelihood to the evidence; Vallinder (2018) says inertia is general; Castro and Hart attack the objectivist reading.
agent_relevance: If 'unknown' is stored as the full range [0,1], new evidence will never shrink it. The flag must trigger fresh sampling or checking, not Bayesian updating.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, section 3.3 Decision making and sequential bets
finding: Credal committee can disagree on the best act, so options can be incomparable. Elga's two-bet case: A loses 10 on heads and wins 15 on tails; B is the mirror. With P(H)=[0,1] each has expectation range [-10,15] and refusal is 0. Refusing both seems irrational because taking both gains 5 for sure.
numbers: Bet payoffs: -10/+15. Sure gain from taking both = 5.
limits: Chandler (2014) and Sahlin and Weirich (2014) show some decision rules forbid refusing both; Elga added an erratum; Bradley and Steele (2014) say rules allowing both refusals are legitimate.
agent_relevance: The agent needs a tie-break rule for when the interval straddles the decision threshold; 'abstain' is one choice but can be exploited across a sequence of questions.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, section 3.5 Regress
finding: If a point value is too exact, why is an interval with sharp ends fine? Higher-order vagueness returns. Williamson (2014) argues for stopping at one precise probability.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: The SEP author answers pragmatically: go only as far up the uncertainty escalator as needed.
agent_relevance: Do not nest 'uncertainty about the interval'. One level of interval is the practical stopping point.

source: Bradley (2019) SEP, sections 1 and 2 motivations
finding: Motivations for IP: Ellsberg choices, incomparable options, weight versus balance of evidence, suspending judgment, unknown correlations, non-probabilistic chances, group belief. Fields using IP include statistics, psychology of reasoning, linguistics of uncertainty (Wallsten and Budescu 1995), neuroscience of ambiguity (Smithson and Pushkarskaya 2015), engineering and AI.
numbers: List only; no empirical numbers in the sections read.
limits: Secondary summary; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: 'Weight of evidence' (how much support) is separate from 'balance' (which way it points). An unknown flag could record weight.

source: Elga (2010) Subjective Probabilities Should Be Sharp, Philosophers' Imprint 10(5)
finding: Elga argues with a diachronic Dutch-book style case that a perfectly rational agent has sharp probabilities. Example of unspecific evidence: a stranger pulls a toothpaste tube, a live jellyfish and a travel toothpaste tube from a bag; what is the chance the next item is toothpaste?
numbers: Sample proposed intervals: [10%, 80%], versus sharp guesses 54%, 91%, 18%. Two bets A (-10 on H, +15 otherwise) and B (+15 on H, -10 otherwise) offered in sequence.
quote: About these matters there is no scientific basis on which to form any calculable probability whatever (Keynes, as quoted by Elga)
limits: The argument was weakened by Chandler (2014) and Sahlin and Weirich (2014); Elga issued an erratum (per SEP). It targets only some decision rules.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-view: a thinking agent that must act on many questions in a row may be safer with point values.

source: Elga (2010), Joyce quotation on motivation
finding: Elga quotes Joyce: symmetric or incomplete evidence should not get symmetric probabilities; the proper response is to hold no precise probability, with indefiniteness reflected in the spread of a family of credence functions. Joyce also says sharp credences are psychologically unrealistic.
numbers: Names Levi (1980), Jeffrey (1983), Kaplan (1996) as earlier sophisticated Bayesians holding this view.
limits: Quote is secondhand from Joyce via Elga. Joyce's own 2010 paper was not retrievable (paywall).
agent_relevance: Matches the design idea: weak, unspecific evidence should give a spread rather than a made-up number.

source: Keynes (1921) A Treatise on Probability, via Elga (2010) and Wikipedia
finding: Keynes used interval-valued probabilities, argued some probabilities cannot be compared or numbered, and gave a version of the two-urn ambiguity example (pp. 75-76, per Wikipedia Ellsberg article). Original text was not opened; Gutenberg and Internet Archive fetches failed.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Secondhand only. Keynes's 'weight of argument' idea is not verified here.
agent_relevance: Historical root of the 'unknown' flag: the weight of evidence is a separate dimension from the probability.

source: Wikipedia, Imprecise probability
finding: History: Boole 1854; Keynes 1921 interval estimates; C.A.B. Smith 1961 lower and upper previsions; Good; Levi; Walley 1991 coined the term 'imprecise probability' on a de Finetti gambling basis. Lower prevision is the highest buying price; upper is lowest selling price.
numbers: Precise if lower = upper for all events; vacuous if lower 0 and upper 1 for all non-trivial events.
limits: Encyclopedia page; does not cover maximality, E-admissibility or Gamma-maximin.
agent_relevance: Gives a behavioural definition an agent can use: 'what would I pay to buy or sell this?'

source: Wikipedia, Ellsberg paradox
finding: Ellsberg 1961 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms' (presented December 1960). Two-urn: 50/50 urn A versus unknown urn B; people strictly prefer betting on A for both colours. Three-colour: 30 red, 60 black-or-yellow; people prefer A over B and D over C.
numbers: Gambles pay 100 dollars. No subject counts given by the page.
limits: Fox and Tversky (1995): aversion shows only when ambiguous and clear prospects are compared side by side (comparative ignorance). Heath and Tversky (1991): competence hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity attitude depends on framing and comparison. Showing the agent a sharper alternative may change its choice; test for this.

source: Fox and Tversky (1995) comparative ignorance, via Wikipedia Ellsberg article
finding: Ambiguity aversion appears when an ambiguous prospect is judged next to a less vague one, and shrinks when judged alone. Not opened; effect size not given by the secondary page.
numbers: None retrieved.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: If the agent only sees one question at a time, ambiguity aversion may not appear; in a comparison it will.

source: Jabarian and Lazarus (2022) A Two-Ball Ellsberg Paradox: An Experiment
finding: Incentivised online experiment: people prefer a risky 50-50 gamble R to an ambiguous gamble AA that always has a higher win probability. So ambiguity is avoided per se, not because it might be worse.
numbers: N=708, nationally representative US sample. 54.9% (abstract rounds to 55%) show the paradox. Mean certainty equivalent 118.13 cents for R versus 101.03 cents for AA; difference 17.1 cents, t=11.7.
limits: Claimed not mainly due to misunderstanding. Cannot be fitted to standard monotone ambiguity models. Related work: Yang and Yao (2017) found up to 45% of risk-averse subjects chose the ambiguous urn in a mean-fixed design; 21.6% preferred a 1-ball over a 2-ball ambiguous gamble in another study.
agent_relevance: Human ambiguity aversion can break dominance. An agent trained on human text may inherit a bias against 'unknown' options even when they dominate.

source: Kuzmics, Rogers and Zhang (2023) An Ellsberg paradox for ambiguity aversion
finding: Lab design close to Ellsberg's two-colour urn with informational draws from the ambiguous urn. Ellsberg-type choices appear at the usual rate but cannot be explained by monotone classical ambiguity models (maxmin, alpha-maxmin, smooth).
numbers: Risky urn 49 white, 51 red; ambiguous urn 100 balls green or yellow; bet pays 10 dollars. 66.67% (18 of 27) subjects made the Ellsberg choice.
limits: Small sample (27). Authors say this casts doubt on classical models as the best explanation of Ellsberg behaviour. Cites a survey of 39 Ellsberg experiments (Oechssler and Roomets).
agent_relevance: Even the formal maxmin or imprecise-probability decision rules do not fully match human behaviour; keep the flag simple rather than copying a human model.

source: Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989) maxmin; Schmeidler (1989) Choquet; Klibanoff et al. (2005); via Jabarian and Lazarus intro
finding: Formal models built after Ellsberg: Choquet expected utility, maxmin EU (choose the act with best worst-case expectation over the credal set), alpha-maxmin (Ghirardato et al. 2004), smooth ambiguity (Klibanoff et al. 2005). Named as background in the opened paper; originals not opened.
numbers: None retrieved.
limits: Secondhand citations only.
agent_relevance: Maxmin is the simplest decision rule on an interval: act on the lower end. The LLM paper below finds model choices align with it.

source: Levi (1980) The Enterprise of Knowledge; Levi (1990) Hard Choices, via SEP and Wikipedia
finding: Levi: belief is a convex set of probability functions (credal set); choice uses E-admissibility, and belief inertia was noted in ch. 13. Primary text not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondhand; E-admissibility details come from SEP citations (Seidenfeld 1988), not primary reading.
agent_relevance: Credal-set belief plus a rule to choose among admissible members is the architecture to copy if an interval flag drives action.

source: Walley (1991) Statistical Reasoning with Imprecise Probabilities, via SEP section 3.2
finding: Walley accepts vacuous posteriors from vacuous priors but says near-vacuous priors that make minimal claims give reasonable posteriors (SEP quotes p. 93). Not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Use a wide but not total prior so evidence can shrink the interval.

source: Yang, Muandet, Caprio, Chau and Adachi (2026) Verbalizing LLM's Higher-order Uncertainty via Imprecise Probabilities
finding: Prompts LLMs to give first-order probabilities plus second-order intervals (PROBINT) and uses a credal set built from an ensemble of LLMs (CREDAL). Standard verbalised confidence stays too uncertain as in-context examples increase, while the interval methods track prediction error.
numbers: GPT-5-mini default, 25 runs (5 seeds x 5 draws), noise p in {0,.1,.2,.3,.4,.5}, ICL examples m up to 80. Vanilla and de Finetti aleatoric scores rise about linearly with p; IP methods stay flat. First-order probability falls inside the elicited interval about 70% of the time; with an added containment instruction, 100%. Approximate MMI correlates above 0.9 with exact MMI and is over 10^6 times faster.
limits: Datasets: MAQA, AmbigQA (ambiguous), MMLU-Pro (unambiguous). Metric AUROC. AUROC values were not legible in the extracted text, so no per-method AUROC is recorded.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an interval-style 'unknown' signal can be elicited by prompting and aggregated across several model samples; ensemble disagreement gives lower and upper bounds.

source: Yang et al. (2026), ensemble credal set and group uncertainty
finding: Group elicitation: lower and upper bounds come from the pointwise min and max across models. The simple averaged score (utilitarian aggregation, the base of majority voting) gives limited power; the credal (MMI) score gives a substantial AUROC gain.
numbers: Figure 5b qualitative; exact AUROC values not readable from the text extract.
limits: Stated at figure level only.
agent_relevance: Disagreement among several samples or models is a usable interval. Majority vote throws that information away.

source: Manchingal, Nikolenko and Cuzzolin (2026) Credal Large Language Models for Semantic Commitment under Uncertainty
finding: Ensemble of LoRA adapters gives a credal set. The model commits to an answer only if its lower probability beats the upper probability of every rival (interval dominance); otherwise it returns the set of answers no plausible predictor rules out.
numbers: Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B on OpenBookQA, CoQA, TriviaQA, ARC-Challenge. Multiple choice: commits on 73-91% of questions at 89-98% accuracy; returned sets of 1.1-1.5 options contain gold on 89-98%; intervals contain observed accuracy in 24 of 30 bins uncalibrated; corrupted context cuts commitment from 87-92% to 65-71%. Open QA: beats semantic entropy and Laplace-LoRA by up to 19% and 9.5% absolute accuracy at fixed coverage on CoQA and TriviaQA with context.
limits: Needs a trained LoRA ensemble (white-box); small open models only. Commit rate trades off against coverage.
agent_relevance: A clear 'commit, or return the set of survivors' rule. A scaffold can imitate it with several samples: act only if one answer's low bound beats all other highs.

source: Mubashar, Manchingal and Cuzzolin (2025) Random-Set Large Language Models
finding: RS-LLMs predict belief functions over token subsets instead of a single softmax vector; credal set size encodes epistemic uncertainty and flags hallucination. Claims better results than standard models on CoQA and OpenBookQA.
numbers: Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B, Phi-2. OBQA accuracy values in the table range 83.2 to 93.0%; CoQA cosine similarity 0.67 to 0.73. I could not tell from the extract which row is standard and which is random-set, so no gain is quoted.
limits: Needs fine-tuning and a clustering budget of focal sets; baseline pairing not verified.
agent_relevance: Shows a belief-function (interval) head is feasible; not available to a scaffold-only agent.

source: Garces Arias, Rodemann and Heumann (2025) The Geometry of Creative Variability: How Credal Sets Expose Calibration Gaps in Language Models
finding: Credal sets (convex hulls of distributions) split uncertainty in creative text generation and compare it with human variation. Models cover little of human creative spread.
numbers: 500 WritingPrompts, 10 human continuations each, 4 models, 5 decoding strategies, 100,000 stories. Best model-human calibration only 0.434 (Gemma-2B, temperature 0.7). Decoding strategy explains 39.4-72.0% of epistemic uncertainty (from the arXiv listing text).
limits: Only the first page of the paper was read; method details not checked.
agent_relevance: Interval width from a model can reflect decoding settings rather than real knowledge gaps; check that an uncertainty flag is not a temperature artefact.

source: Ji, Song and Huang (2025) Credal Transformer, NeurIPS workshop
finding: Replaces softmax attention with a credal attention mechanism (Dirichlet evidence masses) so each layer carries a set of distributions; set size is epistemic uncertainty. Claims fewer confident errors on unanswerable questions via abstention.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract; table values not extracted.
limits: Workshop paper, small authorship team, architecture change that needs training.
agent_relevance: Argument for keeping an 'unknown' signal inside the model, not only at the output; not usable by a prompt scaffold.

source: Helzner (2026) Sensitivity to Subjective Expected Utility Maximization, with an application to LLM decision-making
finding: Softmax choice model with sensitivity parameter alpha measures how closely an agent follows SEU. A 2x2 on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet over insurance-claims triage and Ellsberg-style urns (30 gambles, 4 consequences) with temperature as lever.
numbers: GPT-4o: slope of alpha vs temperature -24.6 [-52.4,-6.7] on insurance, -38.4 [-72.1,-10.0] on Ellsberg. Claude 3.5: -2.9 [-42.9,30.8] and -15.0 [-52.2,19.6]. P(slope<0) 0.99, 0.98, 0.56, 0.77. Robust across four priors.
limits: Author says Claude cells are inconclusive nulls, not zeros; no claim about ambiguity aversion, because it can be absorbed into the belief parameters.
agent_relevance: No clean measurement of LLM ambiguity aversion on Ellsberg urns exists in the sources I could open; an open gap.

source: Daheim and Gurevych (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Generation and Decision-Making Under Ambiguity
finding: Tests Bayesian (expected utility) and risk-averse (worst case over a conformal prediction set) decision rules for LLM tutoring and automatic peer review. Risk-averse rules can hurt by favouring generic outputs; Bayesian methods tend to do better when ambiguity is high.
numbers: Numbers not extracted from the text read; direction of the effect only.
limits: Applies the maximin idea over a conformal set, a close cousin of a credal set. Tasks are subjective, with human reviewers disagreeing.
agent_relevance: Warning: acting on the worst case across an interval can push an LLM toward bland answers. Maximin as the decision rule is risky for generation.

source: Yang et al. (2026), AmbigQA decision-rule alignment
finding: On AmbigQA the LLM's chosen answer matches the maximin and maximax IP decision rules strongly, which the authors take as compatibility rather than proof that LLMs optimise those rules.
numbers: Alignment rates shown in a figure (Fig. 12); exact rates not extractable.
limits: Correlational; the authors state it does not imply LLMs optimise those rules.
agent_relevance: If a model already acts like maximin on its own intervals, adding an interval flag may change little; test it.

source: arXiv listing search for ambiguity aversion and credal LLM papers (2025-2026)
finding: Search found few direct tests: Detecting Ambiguity Aversion in Cyberattack Behavior (2512.08107, uses an LLM to map logs), and Helzner. Credal LLM papers exist (RS-LLM, CLLM, credal transformer, XU-RS 2609.37594, conformalized credal sets 2402.10723). No study found that tests LLM Ellsberg ambiguity aversion with rates.
numbers: Search page results only; titles and gists read, full text not opened for most.
limits: Search coverage limited: other search tools were rate-limited or out of budget.
agent_relevance: The gap is a finding: nobody I could find measured whether a prompted interval or unknown flag improves answers beyond ensembles.
